abstract:
This paper introduces a robust collision detection framework for SDF-encoded geometry, which has seen widespread adop-
tion as a geometric representation in computer graphics. Our approach is designed to satisfy the competing requirements of
numerical stability and computational efficiency of interactive and real-time applications. Our collision management strat-
egy pairs temporal coherence caching with curvature-guided importance sampling. This scheme reliably forms sparse, stable
contact manifolds, even for complex non-convex geometries. Quantitative evaluations against existing baselines demonstrate
significant improvements in both runtime performance and simulation stability. While compatible with a range of numerical
backends, our framework demonstrates how specific solver choices, such as derivative-free optimizers, yield additional gains
in speed and convergence stability. Furthermore, the algorithm is highly parallelizable and well-suited for GPU architectures,
scaling effectively to complex environments containing thousands of rigid bodies while maintaining real-time frame rates. Our
proposed framework is validated through comparisons on complex simulation scenes and ablation studies examining the influ-
ence of various optimizers and sampling strategies.

This paper introduces a robust collision detection framework for SDF-encoded geometry, which has seen widespread adop-

numerical stability and computational efficiency of interactive and real-time applications. Our collision management strat-
egy pairs temporal coherence caching with curvature-guided importance sampling. This scheme reliably forms sparse, stable
contact manifolds, even for complex non-convex geometries. Quantitative evaluations against existing baselines demonstrate
significant improvements in both runtime performance and simulation stability. While compatible with a range of numerical
backends, our framework demonstrates how specific solver choices, such as derivative-free optimizers, yield additional gains
in speed and convergence stability. Furthermore, the algorithm is highly parallelizable and well-suited for GPU architectures,
scaling effectively to complex environments containing thousands of rigid bodies while maintaining real-time frame rates. Our
proposed framework is validated through comparisons on complex simulation scenes and ablation studies examining the influ-

1.  Introduction
Collision detection is a cornerstone of physics-based animation, en-
suring that motion respects physical constraints and remains free
of  non-physical  interpenetration.  While  traditional  pipelines  rely
on  explicit  geometric  representations,  such  as  polygonal  meshes
or  discrete  primitives,  these  approaches  are  often  burdened  by
increased computational overhead, high storage requirements for
complex shapes, and often fail to elegantly handle topological edge
cases [Erl18].
Signed Distance Fields (SDFs), have emerged as a robust alter-
native [MEM
∗
20, PGMAA25, LM24, LZW
∗
24, NE26]. By repre-
senting geometry as a continuous scalar field, SDFs provide im-
mediate access to point-wise penetration depths and collision gra-
dients. However, interactive applications require both collision fi-
delity and real-time performance, thus demanding efficient meth-
ods that can resolve collisions directly using SDF representations.
While  evaluating  simple  analytical  primitives  or  discrete  voxel
grids  is  computationally  light,  complex  representations,  such  as
neural SDFs requiring costly forward passes [PFS
∗
19] or proce-
dural  fields  relying  on  dense  trigonometric  functions,  make  spa-
tial query minimization essential for high-throughput simulation.
Over-generating contact points also degrades downstream contact
solver  performance  by  introducing  redundancies,  increasing  lin-
ear  system  dimensions,  and  inducing  ill-conditioned  system  ma-
trices  [Cat06, AP97].  Furthermore,  existing  SDF  collision  algo-
rithms  are  susceptible  to  local  minima  in  computing  penetra-
tions [MEM
∗
20, NE26], which can impede optimizer convergence
and prevent the formation of stable multi-point contact manifolds,
particularly  in  scenarios  involving  complex  non-convex  geome-
tries [GBF03, TKH
∗
05].
With  these  challenges  in  mind,  we  propose  an  optimization
framework  to  efficiently  identify  concurrent  contact  regions  be-
tween two general SDFs. Our approach generates a stable contact
manifold by distributing a sparse set of contact points across the
intersection volume, rather than relying on a single deepest point.
To encourage spatial coverage, our objective incorporates a repul-
sion term between collision seed points that explicitly reduces clus-
tering at local minima and ensures the contact manifold remains
well-distributed. To address the inherent non-convexity of the SDF
intersection landscape, we employ a stochastic sampling strategy
that is aware of high-curvature regions, based on the Laplacian of
the SDF, where collision is likely to occur. This ensures that the
optimizer is robust to local minima and capable of discovering dis-
joint contact regions, which is essential for capturing the full geo-
metric complexity of the interaction. By prioritizing geometrically
salient  features,  our  approach  mitigates  the  risk  of  local  minima
and ensures a more robust convergence toward a globally consis-
tent contact manifold.
To  summarize,  we  contribute  a  discrete  collision  detection
(DCD)  framework  for  SDFs  that  integrates  temporal  contact
caching, curvature-guided importance sampling, and spatially dis-
persed  seed  placement  (via  repulsion)  to  reliably  form  sparse,
physically stable contact manifolds across complex geometries in
real-time simulation. The capabilities of our approach are demon-
strated  across  challenging  scenarios  that  include  complex,  inter-
locking structures that use both analytical and voxel-based SDFs.
Our method addresses a niche in the performance-accuracy trade-
off space by maintaining physical stability even when utilizing a
sparse set of collision points, making it well-suited for real-time
applications.  An  open-source  implementation  of  our  framework
is made available here:https://github.com/savant117/
sdf-dcd-demo
2.  Related work
The  fundamental  task  of  collision  detection  involves  determin-
ing the intersection state and penetration depth between geomet-
ric primitives to resolve physical interpenetration constraints. The
principles of collision detection and response for physics-based an-
imation  have  been  extensively  documented  in  courses  [AEF22],
surveys [TKH
∗
05] and texts [Eri04].
In this section, we cover prior work on collision detection re-
search utilizing SDF representations, as well as the challenges they
introduce.  We  emphasize  methods  developed  for  interactive  and
real-time applications, where performance is a primary concern.
2.1.  SDF representations
Collision  detection  involving  distance  fields  has  long  been  a  fo-
cus of research in computer graphics. Early work by McNeely et
al. [MPT99, MPT05] introduced efficient voxmap-pointshell algo-
rithms for resolving collisions between point clouds and voxelized
distance fields in haptic and rendering contexts. These approaches
were  later  enhanced  by  Xu  et  al.  [XB17],  who  introduced  Con-
tinuous  Collision  Detection  (CCD)  variants  to  improve  temporal
robustness.
To mitigate the storage overhead inherent in sampled distance
fields, various compression and discretization schemes have been
proposed,  such  as  adaptively  sampled  distance  fields  [FPRJ00,
BMF05].  Koschier  et  al.  [KDBB17]  further  improved  accuracy
by  fitting  local  polynomial  approximations  to  grid  cells.  Work
in  rendering  has  likewise  leveraged  polynomial  approximations
for  adaptive  ray-marching  steps  that  reduces  surface  overshoot-
ing  and  undershooting  [BV25].  More  recently,  neural  architec-
tures have emerged as compact, continuous alternatives for com-
plex shapes [PFS
∗
19, SJ22]. Our methodology remains agnostic to
the specific SDF representation, treating it as a query interface. We
demonstrate  consistent  performance  across  analytical  and  voxel-
based representations, although other representations should pose
no problem.
2.2.  SDF-SDF collision detection
Recent  research  has  advanced  SDF-SDF  collision  detection  by
framing the interaction as a continuous optimization task. Lopez-
Adeva et al. [LM24] proposed a framework for computing inter-
actions  between  convex  bodies  as  a  convex  optimization  prob-
lem  using  the  Ellipsoid  method.  Their  algorithm  derives  ex-
act   minimum   distances   and   penetration   depths   directly   from
SDF representations, achieving performance and robustness com-
parable  to  well-established  support-function  methods,  such  as
the Gilbert–Johnson–Keerthi (GJK) algorithm [GJK88]. However,
their formulation is strictly limited to convex geometry. To handle

more general shapes, Liu et al. [LZW

24] introduced a hierarchi-
cal real-time pipeline that utilizes interval arithmetic for analytic
functions and gradient-based optimization for general fields. Their
method  mitigates  local  minima  by  decomposing  geometries  into
multiple parts via oriented bounding boxes. In contrast, our method
focuses  on  computing  a  persistent  contact  manifold  for  arbitrary
geometries  using  curvature-aware  initialization  and  bypasses  the
computational  overhead  of  hierarchical  bounding  volume  hierar-
chies and shape decomposition. We compare to their approach in
this work. Concurrent work by Nielsen and Erleben [NE26] formu-
late SDF-based CCD as an alternating spatial-temporal optimiza-
tion, reaching sub-millisecond time-of-impact queries for complex
geometries. Our work focuses on the DCD regime, which is com-
plementary to CCD algorithms that focus on determining the exact
time of impact.
2.3.  Continuous optimization for mesh-SDF hybrids
Interactions between SDFs and triangle meshes have seen signif-
icant recent progress through the lens of nonlinear programming.
Macklin  et  al.  [MEM
∗
20]  proposed  an  optimization-driven  ap-
proach to identify the deepest penetration between a triangle and an
SDF by treating the triangle as a compact convex feasible set. The
approach was recently extended by Pelletier-Guénette et al. [PG-
MAA25] into the CCD regime, utilizing both spatial and tempo-
ral gradient information to ensure robust detection for thin, high-
velocity geometry. Although these mesh-based approaches lever-
age the simplicity of the triangle’s geometry to avoid costly projec-
tions, SDF-SDF collisions present a more complex landscape.
2.4.  Warm-starting in simulation
Many  algorithms  in  physics  simulation  leverage  temporal  co-
herence,  or  “warm-starting”,  to  initialize  time-critical  routines
across  successive  frames.  Previous  work  on  the  GJK  algorithm
demonstrated that caching the simplex from previous steps dras-
tically  reduces  iteration  counts  for  distance  queries  of  convex
objects  [GJK88, dB99],  while  Lin  and  Canny  [LC91]  exploited
feature-level  coherence  to  track  closest  points  between  polyhe-
dra. Warm-starting contact impulses has also become standard in
impulse-based constraint solvers to stabilize stacking and acceler-
ate convergence [CB21, AEF22]. Inspired by these approaches, we
apply  temporal  contact  caching  to  SDF-SDF  collision  queries  to
accelerate seed optimization, pairing it with a priority queue selec-
tion scheme to maintain a sparse contact manifold across simula-
tion steps.
2.5.  Implicit operators and field quality
Implicit   surface   modeling   pipelines   often   construct   complex
shapes by composing primitives using Constructive Solid Geom-
etry [Ric73, PASS95], non-linear warping [Bar84], and soft blend-
ing [GBC
∗
13]. While these operators provide expressive control,
they fundamentally alter the underlying scalar field. An exact SDF
satisfies the Eikonal constraint∥∇φ∥=1. However, boolean oper-
ations can create non-differentiable derivative ridges, spatial warp-
ing distorts gradient magnitudes (∥∇φ∦=1), and blending alters

exact scalar fields [BV25].
With regards to collision detection pipelines, these field distor-
tions introduce numerical challenges. First-order optimizers, such
as gradient descent, rely on well-behaved field gradients to resolve
penetration depth and compute contact normals. On procedurally
modeled  or  warped  SDFs,  gradient-based  queries  stall,  “chatter”
along  interior  ridges,  or  diverge  in  non-metric  regions.  Because
real-world physics solvers require stable, reliable contact manifolds
across arbitrary edited geometries, handling inexact distance fields
is  critical.  We  evaluate  our  framework  on  distorted  and  inexact
SDFs, demonstrating robust performance and convergence stabil-
ity even under non-linear spatial perturbations.
3.  Methodology
Our framework solves the narrow-phase intersection problem be-
tween SDFs by algorithmically coupling a robust optimization rou-
tine  with  a  targeted  sampling  strategy.  Potential  collision  points
are initialized via a hybrid strategy of temporal warm-starting and
stochastic importance sampling guided by curvature-based heuris-
tics.  This  strategy  exploits  the  spatio-temporal  coherence  of  col-

for  simulations  of  thousands  of  interacting  bodies  at  real-time

3.3.  Narrow-phase optimization method
We  evaluate  several  optimization  paradigms  to  minimize  the
smoothed softmax objective defined in Eq. 2. While gradient-based
solvers, such as Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) [RM51], of-
fer an intuitive approach given the analytical availability of SDF
gradients, they are often susceptible to stagnation within the local
minima of highly non-linear intersection landscapes. Recent work
has introduced the Ellipsoid method as an efficient technique for
resolving interactions [LM24]. However, its convergence is predi-
cated on the assumption of overlapping convex regions.

3.5.  Stochastic seeding and manifold initialization
Computing the intersection of arbitrary, non-convex SDFs presents
a highly non-linear objective landscape with numerous local min-
ima. Consequently, resolving the single deepest point of interpene-
tration is not sufficient for complex interactions and fails to stabi-
lize collisions between non-convex bodies [GBF03]. Our method-
ology  must  instead  identify  a  diverse  set  of  points  to  produce  a
stable contact manifold. In a large-scale simulation involving thou-
sands of interacting bodies, which characterizes our target appli-
cation,  the  computational  cost  of  dense  surface  sampling  is  pro-
hibitive. Thus our sampling strategy for identifying collision points
aims  to  provide  sufficient  spatial  coverage  to  correctly  constrain
rotational and translational motion, while maintaining a small sam-
pling budget for real-time throughput.
To achieve this, we employ a hybrid initialization scheme that
balances temporal persistence with stochastic global exploration.
We provide the optimizer with initial estimates derived from two
primary sources: (i) cached candidates that leverage temporal co-
herence to maintain stable support across frames, and (ii) stochastic
importance sampling, which is not tethered to historical collision
data and ensures robustness to disjoint collision events.
By seeding the optimizer with this mixture of persistent and ex-
ploratory candidates, we ensure robust convergence toward glob-
ally  consistent  contact  manifolds.  These  strategies  are  described
below.

lations to produce stable contact manifolds across successive time

3.6.  SDF representations
Our framework is evaluated using a variety of implicit representa-
tions. Specifically, we utilize two common paradigms:
Analytical primitives and composites.For basic geometries, such
as boxes, cones, and cylinders, use exact closed-form functions to
evaluate pointwise distances and gradients. These functions can be
combined to create more complex shapes, such as the spiky plates
shown in several of our experiments.
Voxel-based  discretizations.For  complex,  arbitrary  geometries,
we represent the SDF as a sampled scalar field on a regular grid,
a common approach for large-scale simulation [AEF22, KDBB17].
These  volumes  are  computed  from  polygon  mesh  geometry  in  a
preprocessing step. Unless otherwise specified, we use a grid reso-
lution of 100
3
and trilinear interpolation for distance queries.
3.7.  Other details
Following each time step, and to encourage manifold diversity, the
collision  points  within  each  manifoldMare  pruned  to  mitigate
spatial  redundancy.  Despite  the  inclusion  of  a  repulsion  term  in
the  objective  function,  multiple  seeds  may  still  converge  toward
the same local minimum or closely adjacent basins of attraction.
To maintain a diverse and sparse contact support, collision points
found to be within a specified proximity threshold are consolidated,
and redundant samples are discarded from the temporal cache.
For the Ellipsoid optimizer, we additionally warm-start the el-
lipse using the same approach as Lopez-Adeva et al. [LM24]. For
the Nelder-Mead optimizer, the initial simplex is constructed as a
tetrahedron centered onpthat is 10 percent the size of the inter-
sected bounding boxV.
4.  Results
In  this  section,  we  assess  the  performance  and  physical  stability
of our collision framework across a series of benchmark scenarios.
All experiments were conducted on a workstation equipped with an
Intel Core i9 13900H processor, 32 GB of RAM, and an NVIDIA
GeForce  RTX  4090  GPU.  For  the  large-scale  simulation  bench-
marks (Sec. 4.1), we utilize a GPU-accelerated version that resolves
contact  manifolds  for  all  interacting  pairs  in  parallel.  All  other
experiments (Sec. 4.2–4.5) are performed using a single-threaded
CPU implementation. Our CPU simulator implements a velocity-
level, constraint-based formulation [AEF22]. The solver constructs
the  Delassus  operator  using  object  masses  and  constraint  Jaco-
bians, incorporating Baumgarte stabilization to resolve interpene-
tration drift and uses a sequential impulses solver. In contrast, our
GPU implementation adopts the Augmented Vertex Block Descent
(AVBD) formulation proposed by Giles et al. [GDY25], combin-
ing primal constraint minimization using block coordinate descent
with dual augmented Lagrangian updates to stably resolve stiff con-
tacts.  Source  code  for  our  C++  collision  and  simulation  frame-
work is available here:https://github.com/savant117/

4.3.  Penetration depth
We evaluate our framework’s capacity to mitigate geometric inter-
penetration  by  dropping  various  non-convex  shapes–  specifically
the Cow and Bunny models– onto a rigid ground plane and tracking
the maximum penetration depth at each frame. We average the re-
sults over 100 independent simulation rollouts, initializing the ob-
ject with a randomized 3D orientation for each trial.
Because our pipeline pairs a discrete collision detection frame-
work  with  a  constraint-based  contact  model,  which  is  standard
practice in interactive physics engines [CB21, AEF22], minor pen-
etrations  naturally  occur  in  order  to  generate  restorative  forces.
Therefore, to establish an accuracy ceiling, we compare our solver
against  an  offline  geometric  oracle  that  performs  an  exhaustive,
brute-force evaluation using 1,000 precomputed surface points.

4.4.  Energy dynamics
A goal of our framework is to efficiently compute stable contact
manifolds that provide rotational and translational support. In the
absence of a well-distributed support, forces often fluctuate and in-
duce a non-physical “chatter” that is characterized by velocity os-
cillations and poor numerical convergence toward a resting state.
To evaluate the benefits of the curvature based stochastic sam-
pling, we monitor the total kinetic energy produced by bodies at
each simulation frame. This allows us to assess the framework’s
ability to settle and reach a stable state. We compare these results
against a reference baseline using a dense stochastic sampling of
1000 seed points per body, which serves as the “ground truth” for
the energy dissipation profile. We utilize some of the more geomet-
rically challenging scenarios– the Pile of Chairs and Bunny Iron
Maiden shown in Fig. 9 and Fig. 4 respectively. Simulation results
are averaged over 5 rollouts.
